book: $100M Lost Chapters (Alex Hormozi) — compilation of unreleased chapters cut from $100M Offers, $100M Leads, and $100M Money Models

core_frameworks.name: The First Avatar Process (customer segmentation by value)
core_frameworks.summary: Instead of guessing who your ideal customer is, survey your existing customers on demographics, business stats, aspirations, and buying triggers. Sort by who spent the most, stayed longest, and was easiest to work with — keep only the top ~20%. Find what that top group has in common (usually 3-5 traits), then rebuild your marketing and sales process to speak only to those traits and replicate the buying journey that led them to purchase. The same volume of leads sold to a better-defined avatar can produce dramatically more profit per customer without changing the underlying product.
core_frameworks.application: For ClaimFlow, don't guess at 'Medicare agency owners' broadly. Survey/interview the first 10-20 design-partner agencies and call-center ops leads: which ones stayed, referred others, upgraded, or expanded seats? Look for common traits (agency size, number of licensed agents, states served, whether they already got dinged on a compliance audit, whether they use a specific CRM). Bake those qualifiers directly into whitepaper gating questions, ad targeting, and email segmentation — repel the tire-kicker small shops and speak directly to the profile that actually renews and expands.

core_frameworks.name: Attract: Premium vs. Free vs. Discount promotions
core_frameworks.summary: Three distinct 'wrappers' around your core offer, each with different tradeoffs. Premium offers (no discount, apply-and-qualify) generate the highest profit-per-lead and simplest math but need fewer, higher-cost leads and a strong sales process. Free offers generate the most volume and lowest cost-per-lead (Hershey-kiss/penny-gap effect: dramatically more people take something at $0 than at any price above it) but bring more tire-kickers, which you manage by adding friction (qualification questions, more steps, forced content consumption). Discount offers (deep, 50%+, not marginal) sit in between — useful in regulated industries where 'free' claims are restricted, and uniquely good for reducing no-shows via a two-step sale where the prospect already gave a card.
core_frameworks.application: The whitepaper itself is your 'free' attraction offer — it should be positioned as free/high-value with zero friction beyond an email (or company email + role, to filter for decision-makers). Because Medicare/insurance is a regulated space, consider a companion discount offer for the actual ClaimFlow trial (e.g., '50% off first quarter, compliance-first pricing' rather than vague 'free trial') to stay defensible and collect a card, which supports a two-step sale into the paid contract. Meta ads should test both a pure free-whitepaper CTA (max volume) and a discounted-audit CTA (higher-intent, card-on-file) to see which produces better cost-per-qualified-lead once sales works them.

core_frameworks.name: Friction dial for lead quality
core_frameworks.summary: Friction (more qualification questions, more form fields, more steps, forced video/content consumption, longer ad copy) is a dial you can turn to trade lead volume for lead quality. More friction filters out uncommitted people but costs you total reach; the right amount is found by testing, not guessing, and should scale with how much operational capacity you have to handle raw volume.
core_frameworks.application: The whitepaper's gated form is your friction lever. Given the Medicare/compliance angle, add 2-3 qualifying fields beyond email (company size, role, whether they've had a compliance issue) — enough to separate agency owners/ops leads from randoms, not so much that a busy owner abandons the form. For the ad campaign, test a lower-friction 'download now' vs. a higher-friction 'apply to see if you qualify for the beta' framing to see which produces better downstream sales conversion, not just more downloads.

core_frameworks.name: Customer Financed Acquisition (CFA) and its three levers
core_frameworks.summary: The core idea: if the gross profit you collect from a new customer in the first 30 days exceeds (ideally 2x+) what it cost to acquire them, you can recycle that cash to acquire the next customer without needing loans or investors — this is what lets a business compound fast. The three levers are Cost to Acquire a Customer (CAC, spend divided by customers acquired), Lifetime Gross Profit (LTGP, revenue minus fulfillment cost, projected over the customer's lifetime or divided by churn rate), and Payback Period (how fast GP recovers the CAC). CFA has three levels: losing money short-term on customers (level 1, risky), breaking even in 30 days (level 2, capped by your credit limit), and making 2x+ your CAC back in 30 days (level 3, effectively unlimited compounding growth).
core_frameworks.application: For ClaimFlow's launch, calculate real numbers: what does it cost (ad spend + your time monetized + any sales labor) to get one paying agency, versus what that agency pays in the first 30 days (subscription fee) and over its lifetime (subscription x expected retention months). If the whitepaper-to-email-to-close funnel gets you to 30-day gross profit that's at or above CAC, you can safely reinvest ad spend profitably; if not, either the funnel needs to convert faster/higher or pricing needs an upfront component (see one-time fee framework below) to hit CFA level 2-3 before scaling ad spend.

core_frameworks.name: CAC / LTGP / Payback Period calculation method
core_frameworks.summary: CAC is calculated by adding all costs tied to getting customers (ad spend, salaries/commissions of anyone touching acquisition, related software) and dividing by new customers acquired in that period — treat this as a hard, trackable number per channel, not a guess. LTGP requires first finding gross profit (price minus fulfillment cost, expressed as a margin), then estimating average transactions per customer (for one-time/physical products) or dividing gross profit by churn rate (for recurring/subscription businesses) to get lifetime value. Payback period is simply how many billing cycles it takes for cumulative gross profit to exceed the CAC spent.
core_frameworks.application: As a subscription B2B SaaS, ClaimFlow's LTGP = monthly gross profit per agency / monthly churn rate. Track CAC separately by channel (Meta ads vs. organic content vs. email nurture from the whitepaper) so you know which channel to double down on — this is the same diagnostic Hormozi describes running when auditing acquired companies. Set an internal goal before spending real ad budget: know your break-even CAC given your actual churn and pricing, and don't scale spend on a channel until its CAC is comfortably below that number.

core_frameworks.name: Advanced Offer Stacking / Value Grid (the four-stage acquisition sequence)
core_frameworks.summary: Rather than a single linear 'value ladder,' Hormozi models customers as buying different combinations of offers in a grid — some skip straight to expensive options, some buy several cheap add-ons instead of one big one. The universal stacking sequence is: Attract (a hook offer, often free/discount) then Up-Front Cash (a monetized offer at time of acquisition) then Upsell/Downsell (immediate follow-on offers matched to what each person can/will pay) then Continuity (recurring revenue). This sequence can repeat multiple times per customer, and the point is to make sure no one who says 'no' to the main offer leaves without at least being offered something else — maximizing revenue per lead, not just per sale.
core_frameworks.application: Map ClaimFlow's own value grid: (1) Attract = the whitepaper (free); (2) Up-Front Cash = a paid pilot/audit engagement or discounted first-quarter subscription; (3) Upsell/Downsell = higher tiers (more seats, more carriers/lines tracked, dedicated compliance reporting) or a lighter single-user tier for smaller shops who balk at full price; (4) Continuity = the ongoing subscription itself, plus a later upsell to add-on modules (e.g., audit-ready reporting packages, API access for larger call centers). Build the email sequence and sales conversation to walk every non-buyer down this stack instead of losing them after one 'no'.

core_frameworks.name: Offer stacking selection rule: Right Stage, Right Problem, Right Way, Right Time
core_frameworks.summary: When deciding which offer to present, first confirm it matches the current stage of the money model (attraction offers for new customer acquisition, upsells for maximizing 30-day cash, continuity for maximizing lifetime value). Then confirm it solves a real, high-value problem you can actually fulfill. Then present it in the format/method the customer already prefers rather than forcing your preferred solution. Finally, and most importantly, present it at the moment of the customer's greatest felt need, not whenever is convenient for you.
core_frameworks.application: In the email sequence, don't pitch the paid product in email #1 (wrong stage/wrong time) — deliver the whitepaper's value first, let a specific pain point surface (e.g., a described compliance risk or a described attribution gap costing them money), then make the paid-demo offer in the email that immediately follows content describing that exact problem, when it's freshest in their mind.

core_frameworks.name: Freemium as an acquisition strategy (not a business model)
core_frameworks.summary: Freemium works only for near-zero marginal cost products (software) with continuous, ongoing value, where the free tier is valuable enough that people use and refer it constantly but limited enough that real usage naturally creates upgrade pressure. Hormozi is explicit that it's dangerous without deep knowledge of your numbers (cost to serve a free user, and conversion rate from free to paid) and that most people who attempt it get the balance wrong — either giving away too much (never convert) or too little (never spreads).
core_frameworks.application: Given ClaimFlow is compliance/attribution software with real per-account infrastructure and support costs, and the target buyer (Medicare agency owners) is not naturally viral, a true freemium tier is likely a mismatch — Hormozi's own warning against it for undercapitalized, non-viral businesses applies directly. A better fit is the whitepaper-as-free-value-in-advance model plus a paid pilot, not a permanently free software tier.

core_frameworks.name: Free Pick-Your-Price upsell
core_frameworks.summary: Market an offer as fully free, then at the point of redemption offer a sliding scale where the customer can voluntarily pay more for added bonuses at set thresholds. This generates strong goodwill (people feel they're choosing, not being sold), works especially well in low-trust environments, and lets you filter for committed prospects by asking pointed qualifying questions during the 'sale' framed as making sure it's a good fit.
core_frameworks.application: Less directly applicable to core ClaimFlow SaaS pricing, but usable as a tactic for a live webinar or workshop version of the whitepaper content: offer the session free, then at the end offer an optional paid add-on (e.g., 'a personalized compliance gap audit of your book of business') on a pick-your-tier basis, using qualifying questions to separate real buyers from browsers before the sales call.

core_frameworks.name: Free/Discount + Alternate or Paired Revenue Stream
core_frameworks.summary: Give away one thing for free or steep discount and monetize through a separate, related product or fee instead of (or in addition to) the core offer — either a 'paired upsell' (the free thing requires a proprietary paid accessory) or an 'independent upsell' (the free thing naturally creates need for a related paid product). This works because it liquidates acquisition costs immediately and creates a second, sometimes larger, revenue stream from people who declined the primary offer.
core_frameworks.application: Anyone who downloads the whitepaper but doesn't book a demo isn't a dead lead — offer them a lower-commitment paid add-on instead (e.g., a one-time compliance self-assessment report, or a paid 'audit-readiness checklist' walkthrough) so the whitepaper funnel monetizes even the 'no' responses instead of just nurturing them indefinitely with nothing to buy.

core_frameworks.name: Continuity: Lifetime Upgrades (bonus 'when' and 'what')
core_frameworks.summary: To reduce churn on a subscription, layer ongoing bonuses using two variables: 'when' (a time-based delay milestone, e.g., after 4 months, or an achievement milestone, e.g., after a referral) and 'what' (a one-time bonus given once, a variable bonus that changes each time, or a permanent lifetime upgrade/status change). Announcing the type of bonus coming (without spoiling the specifics) keeps customers anticipating and staying. Publicly celebrating status changes (e.g., naming tiers 'VIP,' 'Founding Member') deepens the psychological cost of leaving.
core_frameworks.application: Build a light version of this into ClaimFlow's subscription: e.g., agencies that stay 3+ months unlock a 'Founding Agency' status and a free compliance report add-on; agencies that refer another agency unlock an extra seat free. Mention this loyalty-tier roadmap in the email sequence's later touches to reduce early churn risk once trials convert to paid.

core_frameworks.name: Continuity: Lifetime Discounts with urgency/scarcity
core_frameworks.summary: Offer a locked-in lower recurring price as long as the customer stays continuously subscribed, tied to a believable reason (grand opening, beta cohort, anniversary) plus urgency (limited time) and scarcity (limited seats). Because customers lose the discount permanently if they cancel, this both drives initial signups and meaningfully reduces churn — but only works if you've priced it so you're still profitable at the discounted rate, and you must actually raise the price after the window closes or it isn't a real discount.
core_frameworks.application: This is a strong, direct fit for a B2B SaaS launch: offer a 'Founding Agency Rate' — a genuinely discounted, locked-in monthly price for a limited cohort (e.g., first 25 agencies, or agencies that sign within 30 days of the whitepaper's launch) that agencies keep for life as long as they don't cancel. Use this exact mechanic as the primary CTA across the email sequence and Meta ads: real urgency (small cohort size), real scarcity (limited onboarding slots, framed around your team's capacity to properly implement compliance tracking), and a real reason (early-access/beta pricing before general availability).

core_frameworks.name: Continuity: Discount + One-Time (made-up) Fee
core_frameworks.summary: Charge a steep discount on the first billing period, but pair it with one or more separately-named one-time fees (e.g., 'setup fee,' 'onboarding fee'). This captures up-front cash to offset acquisition costs while advertising an attractive discounted recurring price, and — critically — a larger up-front payment measurably reduces churn (via sunk-cost psychology) compared to an all-recurring, no-upfront structure. If a canceled customer wants to return, they pay the fee again, which further discourages churn.
core_frameworks.application: For ClaimFlow, structure pricing as e.g. '50% off your first 3 months' plus a one-time 'Compliance Onboarding & Setup Fee' that covers the real work of connecting their call tracking / CRM data sources. This both funds actual onboarding labor and, per Hormozi's data point, correlates with dramatically longer customer lifespan than a pure monthly-fee-only structure — directly relevant since compliance-first setup genuinely does require configuration work that justifies a real, not fake, one-time charge.

core_frameworks.name: Presentation-based selling (webinars/challenges/summits) and the three core limiting beliefs
core_frameworks.summary: The more expensive or complex an offer, the longer and more in-depth the pre-sale content needs to be to build enough trust and information to convert (a 60-second ad can sell a $67 product; a two-day workshop is needed for a $100k service). Effective long-form content is structured around addressing three limiting beliefs prospects hold: that results must come easily, that they must get the best possible result, and that results must lead to status/approval. Formats scale from a single free webinar/masterclass (aim ~10% conversion) to multi-day challenges (aim 2-5% conversion) to 3-day virtual summits (aim ~10% conversion on the final day) depending on price point and complexity of the offer.
core_frameworks.application: A compliance-first attribution platform for a regulated industry is a complex, considered B2B purchase — exactly the case where longer-form education wins. The technical whitepaper should function like the written equivalent of a masterclass: address the three limiting beliefs directly (compliance is achievable without becoming an operations burden; you can get complete, defensible attribution, not partial; being ahead of CMS/TCPA scrutiny earns you credibility with carriers and leadership). Consider following the whitepaper with a live or recorded 45-60 minute 'compliance audit-readiness' webinar as a mid-funnel touch before the sales call, benchmarking toward a 10% call-booking rate from webinar attendees.

core_frameworks.name: The Internal Core Four (hiring mirrors customer acquisition)
core_frameworks.summary: Getting employees uses the exact same four channels as getting customers — warm outreach becomes referrals, cold outreach becomes recruiting, posting content becomes posting job openings, and paid ads become promoted job postings — because in both cases you're just getting a stranger's attention and walking them through the same uncontacted-contacted-engaged-qualified-sold pipeline. The 3D training method (Document a checklist, Demonstrate it in front of them, have them Duplicate it in front of you) is the repeatable way to turn a new hire into someone who reliably produces your outcome.
core_frameworks.application: If Steve eventually needs to bring on a contractor or VA to run outreach, content posting, or ad management for ClaimFlow, apply the exact same lead-stage funnel thinking to hiring them (treat job posts like ad copy, treat applicant screening like lead qualification) and use the Document/Demonstrate/Duplicate method to build a checklist for whatever process gets handed off, rather than assuming they'll infer the process.

core_frameworks.name: Maker vs. Manager schedules
core_frameworks.summary: Two incompatible ways of managing time: managers work in small, interchangeable 30-60 minute blocks where an empty slot is 'wasted' and should be filled; makers (builders, writers, engineers) need large uninterrupted half-day-plus blocks because a single meeting can destroy an entire block's usable deep-work time, and open commitments create background anxiety (the Zeigarnik effect) that erodes focus even before the meeting happens. The fix is structural: makers should batch all meetings into a fixed daily/weekly window (e.g., only after 1pm) and protect the rest, and organizations should consider mandated no-meeting blocks for maker-type roles.
core_frameworks.application: Directly applicable to Steve as a solo operator building ClaimFlow while also running GTMVP content: block a fixed 'maker' window for building/writing (whitepaper drafting, product work) and push all calls, DMs, and reactive tasks into a separate 'manager' window later in the day, rather than letting meetings fragment the deep-work time needed to actually finish the whitepaper and product work.

whitepaper_hooks: The real cost of Medicare lead attribution isn't wasted ad spend — it's the audit you can't defend when a carrier or CMS asks where a lead actually came from.
Most agencies aren't losing money on bad leads. They're losing money on leads they can't prove were compliant in the first place.

Position the whitepaper itself as 'value in advance' — genuinely useful, non-pitchy content (per the free-education pattern) that would still help the agency owner even if they never buy anything, building the same trust-before-ask Hormozi describes forcing two pieces of long-form content before a sale converts

Frame the core problem using the 'expensive customer problem' math: if you can't prove which channel produced a compliant, convertible lead, you can't safely spend more than your competitors to win the best customers — and in Medicare, spending confidently is a compliance question, not just a budget one

Use the three limiting-belief structure explicitly: (1) 'defensible attribution can be easy, not an IT project' (2) 'you can get complete, audit-ready tracking, not a partial patch' (3) 'the agencies who get ahead of this now will be the ones leadership and carriers trust with more volume later'

Include a hard, specific number or formula (a CAC/LTGP-style calculation adapted to 'cost of an undocumented lead' vs 'cost of a compliance violation') — Hormozi's own material leans hard on 'money math' as credibility-building, and specificity beats vague reassurance

Close the whitepaper with a stacked, generous next-step offer (per the Advanced Offer Stacking sequence) rather than a single hard CTA — e.g., 'get your free compliance-gap scorecard' as the immediate next step, not 'book a demo'

Subject: You downloaded the whitepaper. Here's the one page most agencies skip.

Late-sequence email introducing the 'Founding Agency' status/loyalty framing (per Lifetime Upgrades) to reduce hesitation for people who are close to converting but haven't committed

An email that stacks a smaller/cheaper next step (e.g., a free compliance-gap scorecard call) for anyone who hasn't booked the full demo — never let a 'no' end the sequence with nothing offered, per the offer-stacking 'no prospect left behind' principle

Use the free-whitepaper-as-hook structure directly: 'Free whitepaper: The compliance gap in Medicare lead attribution' as the primary CTA, optimizing for the penny-gap effect (free dramatically outperforms even $1) to maximize top-of-funnel volume cheaply

Test a second, higher-friction ad angle offering a 'Founding Agency compliance audit' (paid or application-gated) to generate a smaller but more sales-ready segment, per the Premium-offer tradeoff (fewer, better leads vs. free's higher volume)

Speak directly to the qualified avatar in ad copy itself, per the First Avatar process — explicitly name 'Medicare agency owners and call-center ops leads managing multiple lead sources' so the ad self-selects for the right audience and repels unqualified clickers

Use a real reason + urgency + scarcity combination for any discounted-offer ad (e.g., 'First 25 agencies get locked-in Founding Agency pricing before general availability') rather than a generic 'limited time' claim
A retargeting ad for whitepaper downloaders who haven't booked a demo, offering the smaller 'free compliance-gap scorecard' next step instead of repeating the same CTA
